claim: The Dinaledi Chamber within the Rising Star cave, South Africa, contains the fossils of Homo naledi.
source: We describe the physical context of the Dinaledi Chamber within the Rising Star cave, South Africa, which contains the fossils of Homo naledi.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract of the manuscript.

claim: Approximately 1550 specimens of hominin remains have been recovered from the Dinaledi Chamber.
source: Approximately 1550 specimens of hominin remains have been recovered from at least 15 individuals, representing a small portion of the total fossil content.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by excavation data.

claim: The hominin remains represent at least 15 individuals.
source: Approximately 1550 specimens of hominin remains have been recovered from at least 15 individuals, representing a small portion of the total fossil content.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by skeletal element analysis.

claim: The recovered specimens represent a small portion of the total fossil content in the chamber.
source: Approximately 1550 specimens of hominin remains have been recovered from at least 15 individuals, representing a small portion of the total fossil content.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract.

claim: Macro-vertebrate fossils in the Dinaledi Chamber are exclusively H. naledi.
source: Macro-vertebrate fossils are exclusively H. naledi, and occur within clay-rich sediments derived from in situ weathering, and exogenous clay and silt, which entered the chamber through fractures that prevented passage of coarser-grained material.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by taphonomic analysis.

claim: The fossils occur within clay-rich sediments derived from in situ weathering and exogenous clay and silt.
source: Macro-vertebrate fossils are exclusively H. naledi, and occur within clay-rich sediments derived from in situ weathering, and exogenous clay and silt, which entered the chamber through fractures that prevented passage of coarser-grained material.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by sedimentological analysis.

claim: The sediments entered the chamber through fractures that prevented passage of coarser-grained material.
source: Macro-vertebrate fossils are exclusively H. naledi, and occur within clay-rich sediments derived from in situ weathering, and exogenous clay and silt, which entered the chamber through fractures that prevented passage of coarser-grained material.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by sedimentological observations.

claim: The Dinaledi Chamber was always in the dark zone of the cave.

evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by geological mapping and analysis.

source: The chamber was always in the dark zone, and not accessible to non-hominins.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the absence of non-hominin macro-vertebrate fossils and the difficult access route.

claim: Bone taphonomy indicates that hominin individuals reached the chamber complete.

evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by taphonomic analysis showing articulated elements and lack of green fractures.

claim: Disarticulation of hominin remains occurred during or after deposition.
source: Bone taphonomy indicates that hominin individuals reached the chamber complete, with disarticulation occurring during/after deposition.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by taphonomic observations.

claim: Hominins accumulated over time as older laminated mudstone units and sediment along the cave floor were eroded.
source: Hominins accumulated over time as older laminated mudstone units and sediment along the cave floor were eroded.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by stratigraphic analysis.

claim: Preliminary evidence is consistent with deliberate body disposal in a single location.
source: Preliminary evidence is consistent with deliberate body disposal in a single location, by a hominin species other than Homo sapiens, at an as-yet unknown date.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an interpretation based on geological and taphonomic evidence.

claim: The deliberate body disposal was performed by a hominin species other than Homo sapiens.
source: Preliminary evidence is consistent with deliberate body disposal in a single location, by a hominin species other than Homo sapiens, at an as-yet unknown date.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the morphology of H. naledi.

claim: The date of the hominin accumulation is as-yet unknown.
source: Preliminary evidence is consistent with deliberate body disposal in a single location, by a hominin species other than Homo sapiens, at an as-yet unknown date.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and discussed in the manuscript regarding dating challenges.

claim: The Rising Star cave system lies in the Bloubank River valley, 2.2 km west of Sterkfontein cave.
source: The Rising Star cave system lies in the Bloubank River valley, 2.2 km west of Sterkfontein cave.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript.

claim: The Rising Star cave system comprises an area of 250 × 150 m of mapped passageways.
source: It comprises an area of 250 × 150 m of mapped passageways situated in the core of a gently west dipping (17°) open fold, and is stratigraphically bound to a 15–20 m thick, stromatolitic dolomite horizon in the lower parts of the Monte Christo Formation (Eriksson et al., 2006; Figures 1B and 2A).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript with reference to mapping data.

claim: The Rising Star cave system is situated in the core of a gently west dipping (17°) open fold.
source: It comprises an area of 250 × 150 m of mapped passageways situated in the core of a gently west dipping (17°) open fold, and is stratigraphically bound to a 15–20 m thick, stromatolitic dolomite horizon in the lower parts of the Monte Christo Formation (Eriksson et al., 2006; Figures 1B and 2A).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript with geological measurements.

claim: The Rising Star cave system is stratigraphically bound to a 15–20 m thick, stromatolitic dolomite horizon in the lower parts of the Monte Christo Formation.
source: It comprises an area of 250 × 150 m of mapped passageways situated in the core of a gently west dipping (17°) open fold, and is stratigraphically bound to a 15–20 m thick, stromatolitic dolomite horizon in the lower parts of the Monte Christo Formation (Eriksson et al., 2006; Figures 1B and 2A).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript with citation to geological literature.

claim: The dolomite horizon hosting the cave is largely chert-free but contains five thin (<10 cm) chert marker horizons.
source: This dolomite horizon is largely chert-free, but contains five thin (<10 cm) chert marker horizons that have been used to evaluate the relative position of chambers within the system (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript with geological observations.

claim: The upper contact of the dolomite horizon is marked by a 1–1.3 m-thick, capping chert unit that forms the roof of several large cave chambers.
source: The upper contact is marked by a 1–1.3 m-thick, capping chert unit that forms the roof of several large cave chambers.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript with geological measurements.

claim: Cave openings and flowstone-filled fractures do not penetrate the capping chert unit, except where a dextral fault truncates the stratigraphy to the south of the system.
source: Surface mapping indicates that cave openings and flowstone-filled fractures do not penetrate this capping chert unit, except where a dextral fault truncates the stratigraphy to the south of the system (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on surface mapping.

claim: The Dinaledi Chamber is approximately 30 m below surface.
source: The fossil-bearing chamber, named the Dinaledi Chamber ('Chamber of Stars' in the Sotho language; Figure 2A), is ∼30 m below surface and ∼80 m, in a straight line, away from the present, nearest entrance to the cave (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript with measurements.

claim: The Dinaledi Chamber is approximately 80 m, in a straight line, away from the present, nearest entrance to the cave.
source: The fossil-bearing chamber, named the Dinaledi Chamber ('Chamber of Stars' in the Sotho language; Figure 2A), is ∼30 m below surface and ∼80 m, in a straight line, away from the present, nearest entrance to the cave (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript with measurements.

claim: The Dinaledi Chamber is accessed via a narrow, northeast-oriented vertical fissure involving a ∼12 m vertical climb down, with squeezes as tight as ∼20 cm.
source: From the top of the Dragon's Back, the Dinaledi Chamber is accessed via a narrow, northeast-oriented vertical fissure, and involves a ∼12 m vertical climb down, with squeezes as tight as ∼20 cm, to reach the floor (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript with measurements.

claim: An exhaustive search by a professional caving team and researchers has failed to find any other plausible access points into the Dinaledi Chamber.
source: An exhaustive search by a professional caving team and researchers has failed to find any other plausible access points into the Dinaledi Chamber, and there is no evidence to suggest that an older, now sealed, entrance to the chamber ever existed.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on exploration efforts.

claim: There is no evidence to suggest that an older, now sealed, entrance to the Dinaledi Chamber ever existed.
source: An exhaustive search by a professional caving team and researchers has failed to find any other plausible access points into the Dinaledi Chamber, and there is no evidence to suggest that an older, now sealed, entrance to the chamber ever existed.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on geological observations.

claim: Detailed surface mapping shows that no large flowstone-filled fractures occur in the region above the Dinaledi Chamber.
source: Furthermore, detailed surface mapping of the landscape overlying the Rising Star cave system (Figure 2A) illustrates that no large flowstone-filled fractures occur in the region above the Dinaledi Chamber.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on surface mapping.

claim: The skeletal material was collected during two field expeditions in November 2013 and March 2014.
source: The skeletal material recovered from the Rising Star cave was collected during two field expeditions in November 2013 and March 2014, and includes 1550 identifiable fossil hominin specimens as well as six bird and several rodent specimens.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript.

claim: The collection includes 1550 identifiable fossil hominin specimens as well as six bird and several rodent specimens.
source: The skeletal material recovered from the Rising Star cave was collected during two field expeditions in November 2013 and March 2014, and includes 1550 identifiable fossil hominin specimens as well as six bird and several rodent specimens.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript.

claim: Approximately 300 numbered bone fragments were collected from the surface of the Dinaledi Chamber.
source: Of the 1550 hominin specimens, ∼300 numbered bone fragments were collected from the surface of the Dinaledi Chamber, and ∼1250 numbered fossil specimens were recovered from a small excavation pit in that chamber.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript.

claim: Approximately 1250 numbered fossil specimens were recovered from a small excavation pit in the Dinaledi Chamber.
source: Of the 1550 hominin specimens, ∼300 numbered bone fragments were collected from the surface of the Dinaledi Chamber, and ∼1250 numbered fossil specimens were recovered from a small excavation pit in that chamber.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript.

claim: Sediment deposits in the cave become progressively finer-grained on approaching the Dinaledi Chamber from the closest current cave entrance.
source: On approaching the Dinaledi Chamber from the closest current cave entrance, sediment deposits in the cave become progressively finer-grained.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on sedimentological observations.

claim: The Dinaledi Chamber is exclusively filled by flowstone and fine-grained sediment involving two depositional facies distributed across three stratigraphic units.
source: The Dinaledi Chamber is exclusively filled by flowstone and fine-grained sediment involving two depositional facies distributed across three stratigraphic units that filled the chamber over time.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on sedimentological analysis.

claim: Facies 1a consists of unlithified, horizontally laminated, orange mud, with very low sand content.
source: Facies 1a consists of unlithified, horizontally laminated, orange mud, with very low sand content (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript with reference to figures.

claim: The composition of Facies 1a is dominated by fine sericite clay with subordinate amounts of silt-sized chert and dolomite grains.
source: The composition is dominated by fine sericite clay with subordinate amounts of silt-sized chert and dolomite grains (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript with reference to analytical data.

claim: Facies 1b consists of orange-brown mudstone interlaminated with thin lenses of silt to fine- to medium-grained sand with angular to sub-rounded grains of chert and quartz, and abundant micromammal fossils.
source: Facies 1b consists of orange-brown mudstone interlaminated with thin lenses of silt to fine- to medium-grained sand with angular to sub-rounded grains of chert and quartz, and abundant micromammal fossils.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on sedimentological observations.

claim: An extensive search for hominin and other macro-vertebrate bones in Facies 1a and 1b was conducted within the Dinaledi Chamber, but none were found.
source: An extensive search for hominin and other macro-vertebrate bones in Facies 1a and 1b was conducted within the Dinaledi Chamber, but none were found.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript.

claim: Facies 2 consists of massive, non-layered, mud clast breccia surrounded by a matrix of brown mud with localised patches of sparry carbonate cement.
source: Facies 2 consists of massive, that is, non-layered, mud clast breccia surrounded by a matrix of brown mud with localised patches of sparry carbonate cement.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on sedimentological observations.

claim: Clasts in Facies 2 are predominantly composed of laminated, orange-brown mud fragments (Facies 1a).
source: Clasts in Facies 2 are predominantly composed of laminated, orange-brown mud fragments (Facies 1a), which are weakly consolidated, angular to sub-angular in shape, and variable in size, but typically <3 cm in diameter (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on sedimentological observations.

claim: Macro-vertebrate bones, including all the remains of H. naledi, are found within stratigraphic units composed of Facies 2.
source: Macro-vertebrate bones, including all the remains of H. naledi, are found within stratigraphic units composed of Facies 2.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on excavation observations.

claim: Flowstone 1 is the oldest flowstone in the cave and consists of five spatially associated flowstone drapes (Flowstones 1a–e).
source: The oldest flowstones in the cave are a group of five, spatially associated flowstone drapes (Flowstones 1a–e) that appear to be genetically related, and remain as hanging erosion remnants with rounded shapes, near the entrance into the chamber (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on geological observations.

claim: Flowstone 2 represents the most significant phase of flowstone development in the Dinaledi Chamber.
source: Flowstone 2 represents the most significant phase of flowstone development in the Dinaledi Chamber, and forms cascades emanating from fractures in cave walls and the cave roof throughout the chamber.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on geological observations.

claim: Deposits of Flowstone 3 are currently active flowstone formations in the Dinaledi Chamber.
source: Deposits of Flowstone 3 are currently active flowstone formations in the Dinaledi Chamber, and are primarily restricted to the chamber ceiling in the area around the entrance, where they form delicate needle- and rod-like forms that include well-formed crystals of aragonite.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on geological observations.

claim: Unit 1 is the oldest stratigraphic unit preserved in the Dinaledi Chamber and is represented by outcrops of laminated orange mudstone of Facies 1a.
source: The oldest stratigraphic unit preserved in the Dinaledi Chamber, Unit 1, is represented by outcrops of laminated orange mudstone of Facies 1a, which are preserved as isolated erosion remnants in several places in the Dinaledi Chamber (Figure 4A,F).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on stratigraphic analysis.

claim: Unit 2 is the oldest unit composed of Facies 2 sediment and is restricted to small outcrops below the entrance shaft into the Dinaledi Chamber.
source: The next stratigraphic unit, Unit 2, is the oldest unit composed of Facies 2 sediment, and is restricted to small outcrops below the entrance shaft into the Dinaledi Chamber.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on stratigraphic analysis.

claim: Outcrops of Unit 2 contain several, in situ macro-fossil bones that can be identified as hominin.
source: Outcrops of Unit 2 contain several, in situ macro-fossil bones that can be identified as hominin, but are otherwise undiagnostic.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on excavation observations.

claim: Unit 3 is the youngest stratigraphic unit in the Dinaledi Chamber and is represented by sediment that accumulated along the floor of the chamber.
source: Unit 3 is the youngest stratigraphic unit in the Dinaledi Chamber, and is represented by sediment that accumulated along the floor of the chamber and along the bottom of many, but not all of the side passages (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on stratigraphic analysis.

claim: Unit 3 contained dozens of hominin bones exposed along its surface and partially buried within it upon initial discovery of the Dinaledi Chamber.
source: Upon initial discovery of the Dinaledi Chamber, Unit 3 contained dozens of hominin bones exposed along its surface and partially buried within it, in most portions of the chamber where Unit 3 has formed (Figure 6).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on initial observations.

claim: The three samples of Unit 3 from the Dinaledi Chamber are dominated by reworked, angular mud clasts in a clay matrix, with some chert fragments, but with little externally derived detrital quartz.
source: The three samples of Unit 3 from the Dinaledi Chamber (SO31, 34, 39; Figures 2C and 5D,E, 8) are dominated by reworked, angular mud clasts in a clay matrix, with some chert fragments, but with little externally derived detrital quartz.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on analytical data.

claim: The sample from the Dragon's Back Chamber is dominated by detrital quartz, with some detrital muscovite, as well as shale and chert fragments.
source: The sample from the Dragon's Back Chamber is dominated by detrital quartz, with some detrital muscovite, as well as shale and chert fragments, of which some are altered and impregnated and/or coated with Mn- and Fe-oxides.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on analytical data.

claim: The contrasting composition in particulate matter of floor sediments in the two chambers suggests that the Dinaledi Chamber was an isolated sedimentary environment at the time of deposition of Unit 3.
source: The contrasting composition in particulate matter of floor sediments in the two chambers, suggests that the Dinaledi Chamber was an isolated sedimentary environment at the time of deposition of Unit 3, with no or very limited transfer of sediment between the two chambers.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on analytical data and interpretation.

claim: All identifiable, macro-skeletal specimens recovered to date from the Dinaledi Chamber are clearly hominin, with the exception of six avian bones and isolated non-diagnostic rodent elements.
source: With the exception of six avian bones and isolated non-diagnostic rodent elements, all identifiable, macro-skeletal specimens recovered to date from the Dinaledi Chamber are clearly hominin, and all the distinctive morphological aspects of H. naledi are near identical in excavated and surface-collected specimens and are considered part of the hypodigm of H. naledi.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on fossil identification.

claim: The collection of 1550 catalogued hominin specimens includes approximately 1413 hominin fossil bone specimens and 137 isolated dental specimens.
source: The collection of 1550 catalogued hominin specimens (Berger et al., 2015) includes ∼1413 hominin fossil bone specimens, including mandibles and maxillae bearing 53 teeth, and 137 isolated dental specimens.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript.

claim: All dental crowns (n = 179), both from surface collection and in situ excavation, are hominin and morphologically consistent with each other.
source: All dental crowns (n = 179), both from surface collection and in situ excavation, are hominin, and all are morphologically consistent with each other.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on morphological analysis.

claim: The H. naledi assemblage contains many articulated elements, including articulated epiphyses of juvenile limb elements.
source: In general, the H. naledi assemblage contains many articulated elements, including articulated epiphyses of juvenile limb elements, and it contains a high number of infant and juvenile dental and postcranial remains (Berger et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on taphonomic observations.

claim: The avian bones represent lower limb elements consistent with coming from a single individual.
source: The avian bones (UW 101-40 a–f; Aves gen. et sp. indet.) represent lower limb elements (including femur, tibiotarsus and tarsometatarsus) consistent with coming from a single individual.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on fossil identification.

claim: The avian specimens are taphonomically distinct from the hominin assemblage.
source: The avian specimens were part of a group of bones that had been 'arranged' on rocks by an unknown caver prior to discovery by our caving team (Figure 6B), and are taphonomically distinct from the hominin assemblage.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on taphonomic observations.

claim: The hominin assemblage is homogeneous in terms of surface preservation and condition.
source: The hominin assemblage is homogeneous in terms of surface preservation and condition (Figures 10 and 11), suggesting that the remains share a similar depositional history (i.e., the disarticulated vs articulated material does not vary significantly in terms of surface preservation).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on taphonomic analysis.

claim: The structural state of the material is classified as good, and surface morphology is retained for many of the specimens.
source: The structural state of the material is classified as good, and surface morphology is retained for many of the specimens (i.e., no plastic deformation has been observed), even though they were water logged and friable at recovery.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on taphonomic analysis.

claim: The bones are generally, partially mineralised with no evidence of calcite crystal formation in or on bones.
source: The bones are generally, partially mineralised; there is no evidence of calcite crystal formation in or on bones, but some bones and teeth are dotted with black iron-manganese oxi-hydroxide deposits and coatings (e.g., Figure 10), and an orange-colour residue of iron oxide (e.g., Figure 10B).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on taphonomic observations.

claim: Analysis of the weathering patterns of the Dinaledi assemblage indicates that most of the bones show weathering stages 1 or 2.
source: Analysis of the weathering patterns of the Dinaledi assemblage indicates that most of the bones show weathering stages 1 or 2 (after Behrensmeyer, 1978); while 18% have an etched appearance and 11% exhibit dissolution (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on taphonomic analysis.

claim: No element exceeds weathering stage 3 with the majority of elements displaying stage 1 weathering patterns.
source: No element exceeds weathering stage 3 with the majority of elements displaying stage 1 weathering patterns.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on taphonomic analysis.

claim: None of the bone fragments studied preserve evidence of bleaching, cortical exfoliation, delamination or deep patination, indicating that the bones were not affected by solar radiation.
source: None of the bone fragments studied preserve evidence of bleaching, cortical exfoliation, delamination or deep patination, indicating that the bones were not affected by solar radiation (Lyman and Fox, 1989, 1997); that is, no bone fragment was exposed to weathering on surface outside the cave, which is consistent with sedimentation patterns observed in the chamber.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on taphonomic analysis with citation.

claim: Examination of the entire fossil assemblage for fracture patterns indicates that all of the fractures in the H. naledi assemblage resulted from dry bone (or mechanically incompetent) breakage.
source: Examination of the entire fossil assemblage for fracture patterns indicates that all of the fractures in the H. naledi assemblage resulted from dry bone (or mechanically incompetent) breakage, with many bones displaying recent or weathering related (19%) breakage patterns (Villa and Mahieu, 1991; Symes et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on taphonomic analysis with citation.

claim: No examples of spiral (green) fractures have been documented in the H. naledi assemblage.
source: Significantly, no examples of spiral (green) fractures have been documented (Supplementary file 2), which indicates that post-depositional processes are the primary agents of skeletal damage.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on taphonomic analysis.

claim: The matrix sediments surrounding the fossils do not present evidence for sedimentation processes that involved significant water action able to transport coarse-grained material including bone fragments.
source: The matrix sediments surrounding the fossils do not present evidence for sedimentation processes that involved significant water action able to transport coarse-grained material including bone fragments.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on sedimentological observations.

claim: The assemblage presents no evidence of fluvial modifications such as abrasion patterns caused by the movement of bone in water.
source: Likewise, the assemblage presents no evidence of fluvial modifications such as abrasion patterns caused by the movement of bone in water.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on taphonomic analysis.

claim: No element shows evidence of physical smoothing or rounding, the development of polish or frosting, or indications of pitting, denting, and chipping caused by impact.
source: No element shows evidence of physical smoothing or rounding, the development of polish or frosting, or indications of pitting, denting, and chipping caused by impact (Supplementary file 2; Pokines and Symes, 2013).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on taphonomic analysis with citation.

claim: Staining and mineral deposition is common on most elements that preserve an external surface.
source: Staining and mineral deposition is common on most elements that preserve an external surface (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on taphonomic observations.

claim: No evidence is noted of vertebrate modifications such as those caused by carnivores, rodents or other hominins.
source: No evidence is noted of vertebrate modifications such as those caused by carnivores, rodents or other hominins.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on taphonomic analysis.

claim: There is no evidence of stone tool inflicted cuts, scrapes, impact or chop marks.
source: There is no evidence of stone tool inflicted cuts, scrapes, impact or chop marks (White, 2014).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on taphonomic analysis with citation.

claim: None of the specimens are burnt.
source: None of the specimens are burnt (Stiner et al., 1995) or shows signs of trampling other than limited incidental recent breakage by cavers that is readily evident (Behrensmeyer et al., 1986).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on taphonomic analysis with citation.

claim: The collection bears clear traces of invertebrate activity, with most of the bones exhibiting microscopic removal of the bone surface.
source: The collection bears clear traces of invertebrate activity, with most of the bones (n = 553) exhibiting microscopic removal of the bone surface, and evenly spaced, multiple parallel striations (35%) associated with smooth-based pits (34%), a pattern consistent with damage made to bone by modern gastropods.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on taphonomic analysis.

claim: Experiments show that land snails, garden snails, hide beetles and their larvae produce a similar set of modifications to those observed on the Rising Star material.
source: Our experiments show that land snails (Achatina sp.), garden snails (Helix aspersa), hide beetles (Omorgus squalidus and Dermestes maculatus) and their larvae produce a similar set of modifications to those observed on the Rising Star material, characterised by evenly spaced multiple parallel striations (Figure 12A–C), circular shallow pits with scalloped edges and smooth, cupped or striated bases (Figure 12B,E), scraping of the bone (Figure 12D,F), and an etched surface appearance (Figure 12A,B).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on experimental data.

claim: The Dinaledi hominin site represents a depositional scenario that deviates from all other hominin localities in the region in two important ways.
source: Considering the geological and taphonomc context described above, the Dinaledi hominin site represents a depositional scenario that deviates from all other hominin localities in the region (Brain, 1981; Partridge et al., 2003; Dirks et al., 2010; Pickering and Kramers, 2010; Pickering et al., 2011a) in two important ways.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript with citations to comparative sites.

claim: The Dinaledi Chamber appears to have never had unimpeded access, with fossil material deposited in muddy sediment in a geologically and geochemically isolated environment.
source: First, the Dinaledi Chamber appears to have never had unimpeded access, with fossil material deposited in muddy sediment in a geologically and geochemically isolated environment, and second the large vertebrate assemblage is comprised solely of hominin material (Berger et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on geological and taphonomic evidence.

claim: The large vertebrate assemblage is comprised solely of hominin material.
source: First, the Dinaledi Chamber appears to have never had unimpeded access, with fossil material deposited in muddy sediment in a geologically and geochemically isolated environment, and second the large vertebrate assemblage is comprised solely of hominin material (Berger et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on fossil identification.

claim: There is no indication of a direct vertical passageway to surface into the Dinaledi Chamber.
source: Unlike other southern African cave sites where hidden shafts and sinkholes acted as death-traps to numerous species (Brain, 1981; Partridge et al., 2003; Dirks et al., 2010; Pickering and Kramers, 2010; Pickering et al., 2011a), there is no indication of a direct vertical passageway to surface into the Dinaledi Chamber.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on geological observations with citations.

claim: The chert layer forming the roof of the chamber is unbroken and coarse-grained clastic deposits transported by water action are absent.
source: The chert layer forming the roof of the chamber is unbroken and coarse-grained clastic deposits transported by water action are absent, as are externally derived sediments.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on geological observations.

claim: The Dinaledi Chamber represents an isolated sedimentary environment with fossils preserved in fine-grained, semi-consolidated mudstone breccia.
source: Instead, the Dinaledi Chamber represents an isolated sedimentary environment with fossils preserved in fine-grained, semi-consolidated mudstone breccia that is texturally and chemically distinct from fill in the upper chambers of the cave and that appears to have largely accumulated below the current entry shaft into the chamber.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on sedimentological and geochemical analysis.

claim: Sedimentation patterns indicate that the accumulation of Unit 2 with fossils occurred below the current entry point into the chamber.
source: However, sedimentation patterns indicate that the accumulation of Unit 2 with fossils occurred below the current entry point into the chamber, and alternate routes did not involve vertical access shafts that connected directly to surface in either the Dinaledi Chamber or nearby Dragon's Back Chamber.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on sedimentological observations.

claim: The lack of other contemporaneous fauna in the assemblage suggests that the Dinaledi Chamber remained undisturbed by other animals, which could not reach the chamber.
source: The lack of other contemporaneous fauna in the assemblage, and complete lack of surface modifications by vertebrates (carnivores, scavengers or rodents) further suggests that the Dinaledi Chamber remained undisturbed by other animals, which could not reach the chamber.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on taphonomic observations.

claim: H. naledi would have had to traverse difficult terrain to reach the Dinaledi Chamber, with the chamber and the proximal entrance to the chamber positioned in the dark zone.
source: Taken together, this means H. naledi would have had to traverse difficult terrain to reach the Dinaledi Chamber, with the chamber and the proximal entrance to the chamber positioned in the dark zone.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on geological and taphonomic evidence.

claim: The Sima de los Huesos bone assemblage is highly fractured, with most fractures consistent with post-depositional breakage.
source: The Sima de los Huesos bone assemblage is highly fractured, with most fractures consistent with post-depositional breakage, but a small portion (∼4%) consistent with peri-mortem breakage that might be explained as a result of fall-down a 13 m shaft into the cave (Sala et al., 2015a).

claim: Both hominin and carnivore bones in the Sima de los Huesos bear carnivore tooth marks at low frequency (less than 4%).
source: Both hominin and carnivore bones in the Sima de los Huesos bear carnivore tooth marks at low frequency (less than 4%), which has been interpreted as the sporadic action of carnivores trapped after falling into the chamber (Sala et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript with citation to comparative site.

claim: The Dinaledi assemblage shows no evidence of accumulation by either cannibalism or carnivore activity.
source: The Dinaledi assemblage shows no evidence of accumulation by either cannibalism or carnivore activity (Supplementary file 2), making it different from El Sidron, the Aurora Stratum of Gran Dolina, AL 333, and Krapina.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on taphonomic analysis.

claim: The Dinaledi hominins recovered to date are entirely free of cut marks, tooth marks, or peri-mortem fractures.
source: However, the Dinaledi hominins recovered to date are entirely free of cut marks, tooth marks, or peri-mortem fractures while each of these is present at low frequencies in the Sima de los Huesos sample.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on taphonomic analysis.

claim: There are no signals of occupation debris or evidence of occupation within the Dinaledi Chamber, or anywhere else in the Rising Star cave.
source: There are no signals of occupation debris or evidence of occupation within the Dinaledi Chamber, or anywhere else in the Rising Star cave.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on excavation observations.

claim: Sedimentological evidence excludes the transport of coarse-grained material into the chamber by water action.
source: Sedimentological evidence excludes the transport of coarse-grained material into the chamber by water action.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on sedimentological analysis.

claim: The Dinaledi Chamber has been a closed depositional system for a long time, and did not allow the sudden ingress of water and sediment.
source: The Dinaledi Chamber has been a closed depositional system for a long time, and did not allow the sudden ingress of water and sediment; only fine-grained muddy sediment accumulated, which accessed the chamber through narrow cracks that filtered out coarser material.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on sedimentological analysis.

claim: No trace of carnivore damage has been found on the Dinaledi remains.
source: Despite abundant fossil material available for taphonomic study, we have, thus far, found no trace of carnivore damage on the Dinaledi remains.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on taphonomic analysis.

claim: No trace of carnivore remains or the remains of other likely prey animals has been found in the Dinaledi Chamber.
source: Nor have we found any trace of carnivore remains or the remains of other likely prey animals.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on fossil identification.

claim: The sheer number of remains encountered in the Dinaledi Chamber is hard to explain as the result of a single calamity.
source: Apart from this, and noting that the assemblage recovered to date represents only a small part of the total fossil content in the chamber, the sheer number of remains encountered in the Dinaledi Chamber, is hard to explain as the result of a single calamity.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on fossil abundance observations.

claim: The individuals represented within the Dinaledi chamber died at a range of ages from infant to old adult.
source: The individuals represented within the Dinaledi chamber died at a range of ages from infant to old adult.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on skeletal analysis.

claim: In the Dinaledi assemblage, 13 individuals can be assessed for age class, with 3 infants, 3 young juveniles, 1 old juvenile, 1 sub-adult, 4 young adults and 1 old adult.
source: In the Dinaledi assemblage, we presently can assess the age class (and, therefore, the approximate age-at-death distribution) for only 13 individuals, with 3 infants, 3 young juveniles, 1 old juvenile, 1 sub-adult, 4 young adults and 1 old adult (two additional individuals are represented by isolated teeth that cannot be attributed to an age class) (Berger et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on skeletal analysis with citation.

claim: No significant result was found when comparing the currently available age distribution to either catastrophic or attritional mortality profiles.
source: We found no significant result when comparing the currently available distribution to either catastrophic or attritional mortality profiles, and therefore a mass death scenario involving some sort of calamity or death trap cannot be completely excluded to explain the Dinaledi assemblage.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on statistical analysis.

claim: The large number of immature individuals (8 out of 13) allows rejection of hypotheses that would strongly over-represent adults, such as repeated cave exploration by socially isolated adult males.
source: The large number of immature individuals (8 out of 13) does allow us to reject hypotheses that would strongly over-represent adults, such as repeated cave exploration by socially isolated adult males.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on demographic analysis.

claim: None of the bone elements studied shows evidence of green fracture, indicating lack of trauma.
source: None of the bone elements studied shows evidence of green fracture (Supplementary file 2), indicating lack of trauma.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on taphonomic analysis.

claim: The distribution of skeletal material and the evidence for partial articulation could be explained by the slow slumping of fleshed or semi-fleshed remains downslope into the chamber.
source: In this scenario, the distribution of skeletal material, as well as the evidence for partial articulation, could be explained by the slow slumping of fleshed or semi-fleshed remains, downslope into the chamber.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript as a possible interpretation.

claim: The occupation, predator accumulation and water transport hypotheses cannot adequately explain the fossil assemblage.
source: Considering the geological and taphonomic context of the Dinaledi Chamber, the occupation, predator accumulation and water transport hypotheses cannot adequately explain the fossil assemblage.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on evaluation of alternative hypotheses.

claim: Both the mass mortality or death trap scenario and deliberate disposal hypothesis are considered plausible interpretations.
source: Both the mass mortality or death trap scenario (although possibly not involving a single event) and deliberate disposal hypothesis are considered plausible interpretations and require additional investigation.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript as an evaluation of hypotheses.

claim: The preferred explanation for the accumulation of H. naledi fossils in the Dinaledi Chamber is deliberate body disposal.
source: Based on current evidence, our preferred explanation for the accumulation of H. naledi fossils in the Dinaledi Chamber is deliberate body disposal, in which bodies of the individuals found in the cave would either have entered the chamber, or were dropped through an entrance similar to, if not the same as, the one presently used to enter the Dinaledi Chamber.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript as the authors' interpretation.

claim: Reaching even the entrance of the Dinaledi Chamber would always have been difficult, particularly in the absence of artificial light.
source: Reconstructions of the cave environment indicate that reaching even the entrance of the Dinaledi Chamber would always have been difficult, particularly in the absence of artificial light.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on geological reconstructions.

claim: Deliberate disposal of bodies in the Dinaledi Chamber implies that morphologically primitive hominins like H. naledi may have had their own distinctive patterns of behavioral complexity.
source: Deliberate disposal of bodies in the Dinaledi Chamber implies that morphologically primitive hominins like H. naledi may have had their own distinctive patterns of behavioral complexity, even though the reason why H. naledi may have ventured deep into the cave system remains unresolved.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript as an interpretation of the implications.

claim: The reworked nature of the sediments results in mixed stratigraphic signatures that impede faunal dating of the fossil rodent remains.
source: At this point we do not want to speculate on the age of the deposit considering the reworked nature of the sediments resulting in mixed stratigraphic signatures that impede faunal dating of the fossil rodent remains, and the limited amount of clean flowstone suitable for U-Pb dating (Pickering et al., 2011a, 2011b).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript regarding dating challenges with citations.

claim: There is limited amount of clean flowstone suitable for U-Pb dating.
source: At this point we do not want to speculate on the age of the deposit considering the reworked nature of the sediments resulting in mixed stratigraphic signatures that impede faunal dating of the fossil rodent remains, and the limited amount of clean flowstone suitable for U-Pb dating (Pickering et al., 2011a, 2011b).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript regarding dating challenges with citations.

claim: The Dinaledi Chamber was discovered as a result of detailed speleological surveys of a series of chambers known to contain macro-fossils including the Dragon's Back Chamber.
source: The Dinaledi Chamber was discovered as a result of detailed speleological surveys of a series of chambers known to contain macro-fossils including the Dragon's Back Chamber.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Materials and methods section.

claim: When the Dinaledi Chamber was first entered, it was clear that cavers had been in the chamber before, because they had re-arranged some of the bones.
source: When the Dinaledi Chamber was first entered, it was clear that cavers had been in the chamber before, because they had re-arranged some of the bones (Figure 6B), and had left behind several survey pegs.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Further investigation has established only one confirmed entry into the chamber in the early 1990s.
source: Further investigation has established only one confirmed entry into the chamber in the early 1990s (responsible for leaving the survey pegs).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Elevated MnO (3.9–4.2%) and Fe2O3 (10.3–11%) levels in the floor sediments of both chambers are associated with alteration of chert or mudstone prior to their comminution.
source: Elevated MnO (3.9–4.2%) and Fe2O3 (10.3–11%) levels in the floor sediments of both chambers are associated with alteration of chert or mudstone prior to their comminution, with Mn- and Fe oxides/hydroxides occurring as replacement and micro-vein infilling.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on geochemical analysis.

claim: All analysed Mn oxi-hydroxides in both chambers contain fluorine, with similar (atomic) F/Mn ratios of ≈ 0.14.
source: All analysed Mn oxi-hydroxides in both chambers contain fluorine, with similar (atomic) F/Mn ratios of ≈ 0.14, indicating a similar chemical environment during their formation.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on geochemical analysis.

claim: Flowstone samples from the Dinaledi Chamber mostly contain sufficient U for U-Pb dating (0.3–0.7 ppm).
source: Flowstone samples from the Dinaledi Chamber were analysed for uranium to assess the possibility of U-Pb dating. Although analysed samples mostly contain sufficient U for this (0.3–0.7 ppm), a fine dusting of a detrital component derived from associated muds is present in all tested pilot samples.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on analytical data.

claim: A fine dusting of a detrital component derived from associated muds is present in all tested pilot samples of flowstone, which has confounded preliminary attempts at U-Pb dating.
source: Although analysed samples mostly contain sufficient U for this (0.3–0.7 ppm), a fine dusting of a detrital component derived from associated muds is present in all tested pilot samples. This has confounded preliminary attempts at U-Pb dating, because of the high, and isotopically variable, background of common Pb it carries.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on analytical challenges.

claim: The excavation revealed a range of long bones, teeth and various other skeletal fragments as well as a nearly complete, but highly fragmented cranium at the upper levels of the deposit.
source: The excavation revealed a range of long bones, teeth and various other skeletal fragments as well as a nearly complete, but highly fragmented cranium at the upper levels of the deposit, immediately underlain by a nearly complete and articulated lower limb of a child (including articulated tibia, fibula and talus), in turn underlain by a fully articulated hand of an adult.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on excavation observations.

claim: Within the excavation pit the vast majority of long bones were found in horizontal to near-horizontal positions, with limited orientational alignment.
source: Within the pit the vast majority of long bones were found in horizontal to near-horizontal positions, with limited orientational alignment.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on excavation observations.

claim: The horizontal bones were found interspersed with a small number of long bones positioned in a non-horizontal resting state (from near-vertical to oblique long-axis orientations), suggesting a burial history involving multiple depositional events.
source: The horizontal bones were found interspersed with a small number of long bones positioned in a non-horizontal resting state (from near-vertical to oblique long-axis orientations (Figure 9C), suggesting a burial history involving multiple depositional events (Manhein et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on excavation observations with citation.

claim: The fossils of H. naledi were probably deposited over an extended period of time during deposition and reworking of Units 2 and 3, and before deposition of Flowstone 2.
source: Thus, the fossils of H. naledi were probably deposited over an extended period of time during deposition and reworking of Units 2 and 3, and before deposition of Flowstone 2.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on stratigraphic and taphonomic analysis.

claim: Continual reworking of Units 2 and 3 and the fossils they contain is consistent with taphonomic evidence (element distribution; breakage patterns, mineral staining).
source: Continual reworking of these units and the fossils they contain is consistent with taphonomic evidence (element distribution; breakage patterns, mineral staining).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on taphonomic analysis.

claim: The distribution of Unit 2 below the current entry shaft into the Dinaledi Chamber strongly suggests that the current entry shaft has always been the main entry point for sediment into the chamber.
source: The distribution of Unit 2 below the current entry shaft into the Dinaledi Chamber, and the orientation of Flowstones 1a–e that cover Unit 2 and slope into the chamber, together strongly suggest that the current entry shaft has always been the main entry point for sediment into the chamber.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on stratigraphic observations.

claim: The fossils of H. naledi entered via the current entry shaft route.
source: This also indicates that the fossils of H. naledi entered via this route.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on stratigraphic inference.

claim: The presence of articulated, functional anatomical units that conventionally disassociate early in the decompositional sequence suggests that bodies were fresh or in the early stages of decomposition when they entered the chamber.
source: The presence of articulated, functional anatomical units that conventionally disassociate early in the decompositional sequence (Figure 9B) also suggests that bodies were fresh or in the early stages of decomposition when they entered the chamber and were encapsulated in the matrix (Haglund, 1993; Lyman, 1994).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on taphonomic analysis with citations.

claim: The lack of green fractures on any of the elements in the assemblage suggests that the bodies did not enter the chamber due to catastrophic accident such as falling into the chamber or due to flooding.
source: The lack of green fractures on any of the elements in the assemblage suggests that the bodies did not enter the chamber due to catastrophic accident such as falling into the chamber or due to flooding, or suffered trauma in any other way shortly before or after death.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on taphonomic analysis.

claim: Limited weathering indicative of sub-aerial, sub-surface processes in a periodically wet or water-saturated, dark environment indicates that the bones were never exposed to the earth's surface and elements outside the cave.
source: Limited weathering (physical and chemical) indicative of sub-aerial, sub-surface processes in a periodically wet or water-saturated, dark environment (Figure 10) indicate that the bones were never exposed to the earth's surface and elements (the sun and rain) outside the cave (Lyman and Fox, 1989; Backwell et al., 2012; Junod and Pokines, 2013).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on taphonomic analysis with citations.

claim: The fossils experienced significant periods of exposure and reworking after deposition.
source: The preservation of primary and secondary context patterns of skeletal elements, the fragmented nature of many fossil bones, overprinting tide marks of minerals stains on skull fragments (Figure 10F), invertebrate damage on bones by gastropods and beetles (Figure 11), and bone breakage patterns indicative of post-mortem (dry bone) or mechanically incompetent fractures (Lyman and Fox, 1989) probably due to re-working of some of the fossil-bearing sediments (Figure 10) all indicate that the fossils experienced significant periods of exposure and reworking after deposition (Lyman, 1994; Manhein et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on taphonomic analysis with citations.

claim: The multi-staged internment history is best understood in terms of the continual reworking of Units 2 and 3 due to the gradual erosion of the cave floor as it slumps toward floor drains in the chamber.
source: This multi-staged internment history is best understood in terms of the continual reworking of Units 2 and 3 due to the gradual erosion of the cave floor as it slumps toward floor drains in the chamber (the geological process explained above).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript as an interpretation of taphonomic and geological evidence.

claim: The Rising Star cave system is confined to a chert-poor stromatolitic dolomite horizon.
source: The cave system is confined to a chert-poor stromatolitic dolomite horizon.
evidence: This is stated in the figure caption for Figure 1B.

claim: The network of cavities in the Rising Star cave system is developed along west-northwest, north and northwest trending fractures and joints.
source: The network of cavities is developed along west-northwest, north and northwest trending fractures and joints.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on geological mapping.

claim: The main passage forming the Dinaledi Chamber is approximately 25–50 cm wide at its narrowest and approximately 10 m long.
source: The main passage forming the Dinaledi Chamber is ∼25–50 cm wide at its narrowest and ∼10 m long, and expands in width near the intersections with cross-cutting passages (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript with measurements.

claim: The roof of both the Dinaledi and Dragon's Back chambers is formed by the capping chert.
source: The roof of both the Dinaledi and Dragon's Back chambers is formed by the capping chert (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript with reference to figure.

claim: The coarse-grained clastic deposits encountered furthest into the cave are in the Dragon's Back Chamber.
source: The coarse-grained clastic deposits encountered furthest into the cave are in the Dragon's Back Chamber, and include channelized sandstone and quartz/chert pebble conglomerate units that terminate against the Dragon's Back.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on sedimentological observations.

claim: Mapping reveals no large cave openings on surface above the Dinaledi and Dragon's Back chambers.
source: Mapping reveals no large cave openings on surface above these chambers, although narrow, flowstone-filled fractures occur (Figure 2A) that may have allowed passage of water and some fine-grained sediment into caverns below.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on surface mapping.

claim: Stratigraphic units in the Dinaledi Chamber are separated by erosional unconformities, or laterally continuous flowstone intercalations.
source: Stratigraphic units are separated by erosional unconformities, or laterally continuous flowstone intercalations.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on stratigraphic analysis.

claim: There is extensive evidence of reworking with older units being re-deposited into younger units in the Dinaledi Chamber.
source: Erosion remnants of the units occur in a variety of stratigraphic positions, and there is extensive evidence of reworking with older units being re-deposited into younger units.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on stratigraphic observations.

claim: Facies 1a is generally unconsolidated, but contains secondary Mn- and Fe- oxide phases that locally form weakly cemented concretions.
source: Facies 1a is generally unconsolidated, but contains secondary Mn- and Fe- oxide phases that locally form weakly cemented concretions.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on sedimentological observations.

claim: Outcrops of Facies 1a show evidence of in situ auto-brecciation of orange mudstone around exposed margins, due to desiccation, and/or formation of Fe-Mn concretions.
source: Outcrops of Facies 1a (e.g., near the entry point at the top of the chamber, Figure 4F) show evidence of in situ auto-brecciation of orange mudstone around exposed margins, due to desiccation, and/or formation of Fe-Mn concretions.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on sedimentological observations.

claim: The sandstone/siltstone layers in Facies 1b are a few mm thick, and in some places display small-scale current ripple laminations.
source: The sandstone/siltstone layers are a few mm thick, and in some places display small-scale current ripple laminations.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on sedimentological observations.

claim: The horizontally laminated deposits of Facies 1a have been interpreted as autochthonous suspension deposits associated with a low energy environment.
source: The horizontally laminated deposits of Facies 1a have been interpreted as autochthonous suspension deposits associated with a low energy environment as water laden with mud gradually filtered into the cave chamber.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript as an interpretation of sedimentological observations.

claim: Deposits of Facies 1b are interpreted to represent a higher energy environment involving pulses of para-autochthonous and/or allochtonous sediment deposited in the cave by minor sheet flow.
source: Deposits of Facies 1b are interpreted to represent a higher energy environment involving pulses of para-autochthonous and/or allochtonous sediment deposited in the cave by minor sheet flow, which alternated with periods of quiescence during which Facies 1a muds were deposited.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript as an interpretation of sedimentological observations.

claim: Facies 2 locally contains pebble to cobble-sized, angular clasts of dolomite and chert, derived from the surrounding cave walls.
source: Facies 2 locally contains pebble to cobble-sized, angular clasts of dolomite and chert, derived from the surrounding cave walls.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on sedimentological observations.

claim: No reworked flowstone clasts have been observed in Facies 2 deposits.
source: No reworked flowstone clasts have been observed in Facies 2 deposits.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on sedimentological observations.

claim: Facies 2 deposits are interpreted as accumulations of largely autochthonous debris derived from within the cave chamber through weathering and erosion of Facies 1 deposits, or through reworking of older deposits of Facies 2.
source: Facies 2 deposits are interpreted as accumulations of largely autochthonous debris derived from within the cave chamber through weathering (auto-brecciation) and erosion of Facies 1 deposits, or through reworking of older deposits of Facies 2.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript as an interpretation of sedimentological observations.

claim: The typically angular nature of the soft mud clasts in Facies 2 indicates minimal transport and low-energy processes in the cave chamber.
source: The typically angular nature of the soft mud clasts in Facies 2 indicates minimal transport and low-energy processes in the cave chamber.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript as an interpretation of sedimentological observations.

claim: Deposits of Facies 2 accumulated in the area beneath the fissure that forms the entry point into the Dinaledi Chamber, to form a debris cone that sloped into the chamber.
source: Deposits of Facies 2 accumulated in the area beneath the fissure that forms the entry point into the Dinaledi Chamber, to form a debris cone that sloped into the chamber.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript as an interpretation of sedimentological observations.

claim: This debris cone largely developed in the absence of either sustained flowing or standing water.
source: This debris cone largely developed in the absence of either sustained flowing or standing water to explain its topography and the preservation of angular mud fragments.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript as an interpretation of sedimentological observations.

claim: Flowstone 1a is the topmost and thickest (<15 cm) of the early flowstone units.
source: Flowstone 1a, which is the topmost and thickest (<15 cm) of the early flowstone units covers a 10–15 cm thick remnant of well-indurated Facies 2 sediment assigned to Unit 2 (see below; Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on geological observations.

claim: In fresh breaks, Flowstone 1a shows a basal 3–8 mm thick layer of laminated, crystalline calcite, which is covered by an outer layer of mostly white, coarse-crystalline calcite.
source: In fresh breaks, Flowstone 1a shows a basal 3–8 mm thick layer of laminated, crystalline calcite, which is covered by an outer layer of mostly white, coarse-crystalline calcite, which varies significantly in thickness and in places forms a fringe of small stalactites along the outer lip of Flowstone 1a (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on geological observations.

claim: In various places in the chamber, significant undercutting of floor drapes of Flowstone 2 has occurred due to more recent erosion of the cave floor.
source: In various places in the chamber, significant undercutting of these floor drapes has occurred due to more recent erosion of the cave floor, creating hanging sheets of Flowstone 2 (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on geological observations.

claim: In fresh breaks, Flowstone 2 varies from white, coarse-crystalline calcite to grey and brown laminated calcite contaminated with mud.
source: In fresh breaks, Flowstone 2 varies from white, coarse-crystalline calcite to grey and brown laminated calcite contaminated with mud.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on geological observations.

claim: Some of the floor drapes of Flowstone 2 have a sugary texture due to post-depositional recrystallisation.
source: Some of the floor drapes have a sugary texture due to post-depositional recrystallisation.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on geological observations.

claim: Deposits of Flowstone 3 are primarily restricted to the chamber ceiling in the area around the entrance, where they form delicate needle- and rod-like forms that include well-formed crystals of aragonite.
source: Deposits of Flowstone 3 are currently active flowstone formations in the Dinaledi Chamber, and are primarily restricted to the chamber ceiling in the area around the entrance, where they form delicate needle- and rod-like forms that include well-formed crystals of aragonite.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on geological observations.

claim: At some point in time, deposits of Unit 1 would have filled much of the Dinaledi Chamber.
source: At some point in time, deposits of Unit 1 would have filled much of the Dinaledi Chamber, and erosion products (i.e., mud clasts) from this unit are the source for much of the mud clast breccia (i.e., deposits of Facies 2; Figure 4E) observed in the cave chamber.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript as an interpretation of stratigraphic observations.

claim: Small pockets of Facies 1a sediment are preserved in crevices and as hanging remnants, high-up in the Dinaledi Chamber, up to 4 m above the chamber floor.
source: Small pockets of Facies 1a sediment (a few tens of cm long and wide by up to 10 cm thick) are preserved in crevices and as hanging remnants, high-up in the Dinaledi Chamber, up to 4 m above the chamber floor.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on geological observations.

claim: Unit 2 is a composite unit that consists of variably consolidated, clast-supported Facies 2 sediment, dominated by reworked mud clasts derived from Unit 1.
source: Unit 2 is a composite unit that consists of variably consolidated, clast-supported Facies 2 sediment, dominated by reworked mud clasts derived from Unit 1, mixed with rare chert and dolomite fragments (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on stratigraphic analysis.

claim: The mud clasts in Unit 2 are composed of a combination of fresh (orange), angular clasts, and more oxidized (brown), sub-angular to sub-rounded clasts.
source: The mud clasts in this unit are composed of a combination of fresh (orange), angular clasts, and more oxidized (brown), sub-angular to sub-rounded clasts (Figure 4E), set in an oxidized, brown muddy matrix with some silt- to sand-sized particles, and locally cemented by sparry carbonate.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on sedimentological observations.

claim: Outcrops of Unit 2 are preserved as erosional remnants of limited size that are attached below the hanging aprons of Flowstones 1a–e.
source: Outcrops of Unit 2 are preserved as erosional remnants of limited size that are attached below the hanging aprons of Flowstones 1a–e.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on stratigraphic observations.

claim: The topmost outcrop of Unit 2 occurs below Flowstone 1a, and consists of a 10–15 cm thick erosion remnant of consolidated mud clast breccia.
source: The topmost outcrop of Unit 2 occurs below Flowstone 1a, and consists of a 10–15 cm thick erosion remnant of consolidated mud clast breccia (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on stratigraphic observations.

claim: The outer surface of the topmost outcrop of Unit 2 has a smooth appearance as a result of dissolution after deposition and lithification.
source: The outer surface of this outcrop has a smooth appearance as a result of dissolution after deposition and lithification.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on geological observations.

claim: Erosion remnants of Unit 2 that are preserved underneath aprons of Flowstones 1b–e are mostly unconsolidated and have a rubbly appearance.
source: In contrast, erosion remnants of Unit 2 that are preserved underneath aprons of Flowstones 1b–e (Figure 4C), are mostly unconsolidated and have a rubbly appearance.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on geological observations.

claim: Outcrops of Unit 2 dip southwest at approximately 20–30° into the Dinaledi Chamber.
source: Like the overlying flowstone sheets, outcrops of Unit 2 dip southwest at ∼20–30° into the Dinaledi Chamber (Figure 4C), which indicates that Unit 2 accumulated on a debris cone or rubble deposit that sloped into the chamber and developed below the entry shaft.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on stratigraphic observations.

claim: Unit 3 is composed of largely unconsolidated sediment of Facies 2 dominated by reworked orange mud clasts embedded in a brown muddy matrix.
source: Unit 3 is the youngest stratigraphic unit in the Dinaledi Chamber, and is represented by sediment that accumulated along the floor of the chamber and along the bottom of many, but not all of the side passages (Figure 4G). Unit 3 is composed of largely unconsolidated sediment of Facies 2 dominated by reworked orange mud clasts embedded in a brown muddy matrix.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on stratigraphic and sedimentological observations.

claim: Unit 3 is massive and displays no evidence of layering or grading, and is commonly matrix supported.
source: This unit is massive and displays no evidence of layering or grading, and is commonly matrix supported (as opposed to the mostly clast-supported Unit 2).

claim: Unit 3 has been derived from weathering and erosion of Units 1 and 2.
source: It has been derived from weathering and erosion of Units 1 and 2.

claim: Unit 3 partly covers exposures of Unit 1 in several side passages and near the entry point into the cave.
source: Unit 3 partly covers exposures of Unit 1 in several side passages and near the entry point into the cave.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on stratigraphic observations.

claim: A series of minor test pits were dug into Unit 3 at various areas of the cave floor, which revealed that abundant additional hominin bones are buried at shallow depths within Unit 3 throughout much of the chamber.
source: A series of minor test pits (a few cm deep) were dug into Unit 3 at various areas of the cave floor, which revealed that abundant additional hominin bones are buried at shallow depths within Unit 3 throughout much of the chamber.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on excavation observations.

claim: Unit 3 also contains rare disarticulated rodent remains that are undiagnostic of age.

claim: In many parts of the chamber, Unit 3 is covered by a thin sheet of Flowstone 2.
source: In many parts of the chamber, Unit 3 is covered by a thin sheet of Flowstone 2, which spread across the top of Unit 3 from a number of separate drip points.

source: The formation of drapes of Flowstone 2 atop Unit 3 was followed by localized, post-depositional erosion of the cave floor, a process that continues today, as sediment is periodically washed down floor drains in the chamber.

claim: Hanging erosion remnants of Flowstone 2 are preserved in several places along the walls of the cave chamber up to 20 cm above the present cave floor.
source: As a result, hanging erosion remnants of Flowstone 2 are preserved in several places along the walls of the cave chamber (e.g., directly north of the excavation pit), where they remain up to 20 cm above the present cave floor (Figure 4F,G).

claim: Four samples of cave sediment were studied using different techniques to obtain data on their size fraction, mineralogy and geochemical characteristics.

source: XRD diffractograms identified both quartz and muscovite in all samples with high scores compared to other minerals.

claim: Hematite was identified with high scores in all the Dinaledi samples.
source: Hematite was identified with high scores in all the Dinaledi samples.
