claim: Acid tests showed all samples to be free of calcite or aragonite.
source: Acid tests showed all samples to be free of calcite or aragonite.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on analytical data.

claim: The Dinaledi Chamber collection displays taphonomic characteristics indicative of a depositional history that involved several stages of burial.
source: The Dinaledi collection displays taphonomic characteristics indicative of a depositional history that involved several stages of burial with surface modifications and breakage patterns consistent with repeated reworking of at least part of the assemblage within the confines of the Dinaledi Chamber, involving both biotic and abiotic agents (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on taphonomic analysis.

claim: The distribution of bone material and skeletal part representation indicative of limited winnowing indicate that the fossils of H. naledi must have found their way into the chamber via a difficult route that precluded any other large vertebrates from finding a way in.
source: The distribution of bone material and skeletal part representation indicative of limited winnowing (Table 1) indicate that the fossils of H. naledi must have found their way into the chamber via a difficult route that precluded any other large vertebrates from finding a way in.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on taphonomic analysis.

claim: The distribution of the fossils within reworked material derived from Unit 2, as well-articulated remains in Unit 3 suggests that H. naledi fossils entered the chamber over an extended period of time.
source: The distribution of the fossils within reworked material derived from Unit 2, as well-articulated remains in Unit 3 suggests that H. naledi fossils entered the chamber over an extended period of time; that is, not all remains were deposited at once.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on stratigraphic and taphonomic analysis.

claim: The collection is notable for the absence of large vertebrate remains.
source: The collection is also notable for the absence of large vertebrate remains, and the taphonomic processes that are not evidenced through surface and structural modifications and skeletal part representation most importantly there is no evidence for carnivore or rodent modification; no evidence of cut marks or burns and no (geological or taphonomic) traces of fluvial transportation or long-distance movement or traces of green bone fractures (Haglund, 1992; Lyman, 1994; Fernández-Jalvo and Andrews, 2003; Pickering et al., 2011a).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on taphonomic analysis with citations.

claim: Mono-specific assemblages have been described from Tertiary and Mesozoic vertebrate fossil sites, linked to catastrophic events.
source: Mono-specific assemblages have been described from Tertiary and Mesozoic vertebrate fossil sites (Kidwell et al., 1986; Rogers, 1990; Behrensmeyer, 1991), linked to catastrophic events (Turnbull and Martill, 1988).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript with citations to comparative studies.

claim: Among deposits of non H. sapiens hominins, where evidence of catastrophic events is lacking, mono-specific assemblages have been associated typically with deliberate cultural deposition or burial.
source: Among deposits of non H. sapiens hominins, where evidence of catastrophic events is lacking, mono-specific assemblages have been associated typically with deliberate cultural deposition or burial (Arsuaga et al., 1997; Carbonell and Mosquera, 2006; Gaudzinski, 2006).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript with citations to comparative studies.

claim: Every previously known case of cultural deposition has been attributed to species of the genus Homo with cranial capacities near the modern human range.
source: Every previously known case of cultural deposition has been attributed to species of the genus Homo with cranial capacities near the modern human range.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on review of literature.

claim: The fossil hominins from Sima de los Huesos, Atapuerca, Spain, are presently believed to have accumulated within a single event.
source: The fossil hominins from Sima de los Huesos, Atapuerca, Spain, are presently believed to have accumulated within a single event (Aranburu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript with citation to comparative site.

claim: The Sima de los Huesos assemblage also includes carnivore remains, including the remains of an extensive number of cave bears and smaller carnivores.
source: The assemblage also includes carnivore remains, including the remains of (an extensive number of) cave bears and smaller carnivores.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript regarding the comparative site.

claim: Cut marks have not been reported on the hominin remains from Sima de los Huesos.
source: Cut marks have not been reported on the hominin remains (Andrews and Jalvo, 1997).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript with citation to comparative site.

claim: Level TD6-2 of Gran Dolina, Spain, represents an accumulation of hominin and faunal bones in a approximately 30 cm thick layer across an excavated extent of 7 m2.
source: Another example is presented by Level TD6-2 of Gran Dolina, Spain, which represents an accumulation of hominin and faunal bones in a ∼30 cm thick layer across an excavated extent of 7 m2.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript regarding a comparative site.

claim: The remains of at least six hominin individuals are present in the Gran Dolina TD6-2 assemblage.
source: The remains of at least six hominin individuals are present in this assemblage, with cut marks and evidence of intentional de-fleshing similar to associated fauna, as well as tooth marks from carnivores (Saladié et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript with citation to comparative site.

claim: The Gran Dolina TD6-2 accumulation of hominin bone is interpreted as the result of cannibalism, with later carnivore scavenging at a smaller scale.
source: The accumulation of hominin bone is interpreted as the result of cannibalism, with later carnivore scavenging at a smaller scale.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript with citation to comparative site.

claim: At El Sidron, Spain, an almost exclusively hominin assemblage comprises a minimum of 13 individuals bearing cut marks, percussion pitting, and conchoidal scars typical of intentional processing of carcasses.
source: A similar instance of cannibalism appears to be evidenced at El Sidron, Spain. Here, an almost exclusively hominin assemblage comprises a minimum of 13 individuals bearing cut marks, percussion pitting, and conchoidal scars typical of intentional processing of carcasses (Rosas et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript with citation to comparative site.

claim: The Krapina rock shelter in Croatia represents the earliest-excavated large hominin sample with remains of a minimum of 23 individual Hominins.
source: The Krapina rock shelter in Croatia represents the earliest-excavated large hominin sample. Here remains of a minimum of 23 individual Hominins were recovered with extensive associated fauna from several stratigraphic layers, with most hominin material coming from a single layer, the 'Homo Zonus'.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript regarding a comparative site.

claim: Breakage patterns of the Krapina hominin assemblage are mostly consistent with post-depositional fracturing, including excavation damage and prehistoric fracturing due to sedimentary loading.
source: Breakage patterns of the Krapina hominin assemblage are mostly consistent with post-depositional fracturing, including excavation damage and prehistoric fracturing due to sedimentary loading (Russell, 1987a).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript with citation to comparative site.

claim: Many of the hominin bones from Krapina bear cut marks, which have been variably interpreted as evidence of cannibalism or mortuary practices.
source: Many of the hominin bones bear cut marks, which have been variably interpreted as evidence of cannibalism or mortuary practices (Russell, 1987b; Villa, 1992).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript with citations to comparative site.

claim: The AL 333 assemblage from Hadar, Ethiopia includes the fragmentary remains of some 17 hominin individuals and fauna, which appear to have been redeposited within a shallow streambed after possibly having been subject to predation.
source: The AL 333 assemblage from Hadar, Ethiopia includes the fragmentary remains of some 17 hominin individuals and fauna, which appear to have been redeposited within a shallow streambed after possibly having been subject to predation (Behrensmeyer, 2008).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript with citation to comparative site.

claim: Malapa, in the Cradle of Humankind, South Africa has been interpreted as a 'death trap', with several partial hominin skeletons and associated fauna.
source: Malapa, in the Cradle of Humankind, South Africa has been interpreted as a 'death trap', with several partial hominin skeletons and associated fauna (Dirks et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript with citation to comparative site.

claim: The Malapa hominin and faunal assemblages lack evidence of carnivore activity.
source: The Malapa hominin and faunal assemblages lack evidence of carnivore activity, and include a disproportionate fraction of climbing species, suggesting that access to the cave was formerly limited and possibly hazardous for ungulates (Val et al., 2015), but a broad array of faunal species have been recovered from the site.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript with citation to comparative site.

claim: The Dinaledi situation shows similarities with the Sima de los Huesos assemblage in several respects.
source: The Dinaledi situation shows similarities with the Sima de los Huesos assemblage in several respects.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript as a comparison.

claim: Few previously recognised scenarios operating in South African caves could have produced the selectivity for hominin remains as observed in the Dinaledi Chamber.
source: Few previously recognised scenarios operating in South African caves could have produced the selectivity for hominin remains as observed in the Dinaledi Chamber (Brain, 1981; de Ruiter and Berger, 2000; Dirks et al., 2010); a depositional situation common in no species other than modern humans.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript with citations.

claim: If hominins were traveling to the chamber, it is assumed that they would almost certainly have required artificial light.
source: Based on our current assessment, occupation would have required accessing the chamber in the dark through an entrance similar to the current one, through an area inaccessible to other medium- to large-sized mammals. Thus, if hominins were traveling to the chamber, it is assumed that they would almost certainly have required artificial light.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript as an inference about occupation hypothesis.

claim: Given the physical challenges associated with access into the chamber and the lack of evidence for longer-term use, occupation is considered an unlikely explanation for the presence of the hominin remains.
source: Given the physical challenges associated with access into the chamber and the lack of evidence for longer-term use, we consider occupation an unlikely explanation for the presence of the hominin remains.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript as an evaluation of the occupation hypothesis.

claim: The cave has been inundated in the past by rising water tables.
source: The cave has been inundated in the past by rising water tables, but there is no evidence within the Dinaledi Chamber of depositional processes that involved high-energy transport mechanisms capable of transporting the large hominin bones, let alone do so in a uniquely selective manner.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on geological observations.

claim: The high abundance and diversity of predominantly non-hominin fossil remains preserved throughout the adjacent Dragon's Back Chamber refute sediment transport by water flow between the two chambers.
source: The high abundance and diversity of predominantly non-hominin fossil remains preserved throughout the adjacent Dragon's Back Chamber not only refute sediment transport by water flow between the two chambers, but also indicates that a considerable barrier between the two chambers was in place at time of deposition of H. naledi, and indeed throughout the history of the Dinaledi Chamber.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on fossil distribution and sedimentological analysis.

claim: The accumulation of the hominin remains in the chamber does not fit the pattern of a flood or fluvial event.
source: Thus, the accumulation of the hominin remains in the chamber does not fit the pattern of a flood or fluvial event (Behrensmeyer, 2008; Dirks et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript with citations.

claim: In the predator accumulation hypothesis a carnivore would need to overcome the challenges of navigating the dark zone of the cave in order to access a remote chamber, all while transporting a large hominin carcass.
source: In this hypothesis a carnivore either killed or scavenged the hominins, and brought them into the Dinaledi Chamber. In doing so, the predator would need to overcome the challenges of navigating the dark zone of the cave described earlier, in order to access a remote chamber, all while transporting a large hominin carcass.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript as an evaluation of the predator accumulation hypothesis.

claim: The predator would have had to select a single prey species—H. naledi—carrying into the chamber all age and size categories without leaving a trace of its own presence.
source: Thus, the predator would have had to select a single prey species—H. naledi—carrying into the chamber all age and size categories (Berger et al., 2015) without leaving a trace of its own presence. We consider this very unlikely.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript as an evaluation of the predator accumulation hypothesis with citation.

claim: The sedimentological evidence presented suggests that accumulation of the fossils occurred over a period of time during deposition and reworking of Units 2, and 3, which refutes a single event hypothesis.
source: The sedimentological evidence presented suggests that accumulation of the fossils occurred over a period of time during deposition and reworking of Units 2, and 3, which refutes a single event hypothesis.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on sedimentological analysis.

claim: The individual entry hypothesis would require individuals or small groups to enter repeatedly and succumb to some form of, as yet unidentified, mortality event.
source: The individual entry hypothesis would require individuals or small groups to enter repeatedly and succumb to some form of, as yet unidentified, mortality event.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript as an evaluation of the death trap hypothesis.

claim: The demographics of the assemblage—which includes individuals of practically every developmental age, from neonate to senile, is inconclusive in terms of providing definitive evidence towards either attritional or catastrophic mass fatality events.
source: The demographics of the assemblage—which includes individuals of practically every developmental age, from neonate to senile, is inconclusive in terms of providing definitive evidence towards either attritional or catastrophic mass fatality events.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript based on demographic analysis.

claim: The mortality profiles of the Sima de los Huesos and Krapina hominin samples have been argued as consistent with a catastrophic profile using statistical tests.
source: The mortality profiles of the Sima de los Huesos and Krapina hominin samples have been argued as consistent with a catastrophic profile using statistical tests (Bocquet-Appel and Arsuaga, 1999).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript with citation to comparative analysis.

claim: In both the Krapina and Sima de los Huesos assemblages, sample sizes are small and near the numerical limit to test statistically.
source: In both the Krapina and Sima de los Huesos assemblages, sample sizes are small and near the numerical limit to test statistically.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript regarding comparative sites.

claim: If bodies were dropped down the entrance, it is unlikely that they would have fallen rapidly, or landed with any force.
source: None of the bone elements studied shows evidence of green fracture (Supplementary file 2), indicating lack of trauma. Therefore, if bodies were dropped down the entrance, it is unlikely that they would have fallen rapidly, or landed with any force; perhaps because the entry is too irregular and narrow to allow a body to freefall and gain speed, or perhaps because a pile of soft muddy sediment had accumulated below the entry way, breaking the momentum of any falling object.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript as an interpretation of taphonomic evidence.

claim: Accessing the entry point to the chamber to drop bodies down the chute would have still entailed a complex climb in the dark zone.
source: Note that accessing the entry point to the chamber to drop bodies down the chute would have still entailed a complex climb in the dark zone.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript as an observation about the deliberate disposal hypothesis.

claim: The hominins could have entered the chamber directly, carrying the bodies or dying there, which would explain the absence of green fractures and the presence of delicate, articulated remains in the excavation pit.
source: Alternatively, the hominins could have entered the chamber directly, carrying the bodies or dying there, which would explain, not only the absence of green fractures, but the presence of delicate, articulated remains in the excavation pit, deep in the chamber, well away from the entrance point, on the other side of floor drains.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript as an alternative interpretation.

claim: Recent evidence has extended the record of complex behaviour from archaic and modern humans to earlier hominins.
source: Recent evidence has extended the record of complex behaviour from archaic and modern humans (Haglund, 1993; Arsuaga et al., 1997; Carbonell and Mosquera, 2006) to earlier hominins (McBreaty and Brooks, 2000; Douka and Spinapolice, 2012; Joordens et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript with citations to literature.

claim: The reason why H. naledi may have ventured deep into the cave system remains unresolved.
source: Deliberate disposal of bodies in the Dinaledi Chamber implies that morphologically primitive hominins like H. naledi may have had their own distinctive patterns of behavioral complexity, even though the reason why H. naledi may have ventured deep into the cave system remains unresolved.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript.

source: Further method development is underway to circumvent this problem.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript regarding future work.

source: Prior to our work there is no evidence that excavations for fossils were ever undertaken in the Rising Star cave.
